paths.name: Persian Gulf Crude Oil via the Strait of Hormuz
chokepoints: Strait of Hormuz
paths.why_it_matters: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's single largest oil chokepoint by volume, carrying roughly a fifth of global petroleum consumption and about a quarter of all globally traded seaborne oil. It is also a major LNG artery, since Qatar's exports must transit the strait. Because the strait is narrow and has no full-capacity bypass, any disruption has outsized effects on global oil prices and shipping insurance costs.
historical_precedents: A 1980s campaign of attacks on commercial tankers in the Persian Gulf led Lloyd's of London and other insurers to sharply raise war-risk insurance premiums on Gulf-transiting tankers, cut Gulf shipping volumes by roughly a quarter, and contributed to oil-price volatility through the mid-to-late 1980s.
paths.estimated_global_share: About 20.9 million barrels per day transited the Strait of Hormuz in the first half of 2025, roughly 20% of global petroleum consumption and about a quarter of total global maritime-traded oil, plus over 20% of global LNG trade, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

paths.name: Strait of Malacca Oil and LNG Corridor to East Asia
chokepoints: Strait of Malacca
paths.why_it_matters: The Strait of Malacca is the shortest sea route linking Middle East and African suppliers to East and Southeast Asian markets, and by the U.S. Energy Information Administration's 1H2025 data it is now the single largest oil transit chokepoint in the world by volume, ahead of the Strait of Hormuz. At its narrowest point (the Phillips Channel) it is only about 1.7 miles wide, making it vulnerable to collisions, groundings, and piracy, with no practical alternative route for most of this traffic short of a lengthy detour around the Indonesian archipelago.
historical_precedents: EIA has tracked a multi-year rise in Malacca throughput, from about 16 million barrels per day in 2016 (a fourth consecutive annual increase at the time) to 23.2 million barrels per day in the first half of 2025, reflecting the strait's growing centrality to global oil and LNG trade.
paths.estimated_global_share: 23.2 million barrels per day of oil transited the Strait of Malacca in 1H2025 (about 29% of total global maritime oil flows), plus 9.2 billion cubic feet per day of LNG, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

paths.name: Suez Canal and SUMED Pipeline Corridor
chokepoints: Suez Canal
SUMED Pipeline
paths.why_it_matters: The Suez Canal and the parallel SUMED overland pipeline together form the primary direct sea link between the Arabian/Indian Ocean basin and the Mediterranean, letting tankers avoid the much longer voyage around the southern tip of Africa. SUMED alone can carry up to 2.8 million barrels per day when the canal is congested or too shallow for very large tankers, and the corridor also carries a meaningful share of global LNG trade.
historical_precedents: The container ship Ever Given ran aground and blocked the Suez Canal for about six days in March 2021, halting an estimated several billion dollars per day of transiting trade (Lloyd's List estimated roughly $400 million per hour) and forcing dozens of vessels to wait or divert.

Beginning in late 2023, security incidents affecting commercial shipping in the Red Sea prompted many carriers to reroute around the Cape of Good Hope; by mid-October 2024 average daily Suez Canal transits had fallen about 57% from their peak and roughly 55% year-over-year, per UNCTAD.
paths.estimated_global_share: Combined Suez Canal and SUMED pipeline oil flows were about 4.9 million barrels per day in 1H2025 (roughly 6% of total seaborne-traded oil), down from about 12% of seaborne-traded oil in 1H2023 due to Red Sea rerouting, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

paths.name: Bab-el-Mandeb Strait Oil and LNG Flows
chokepoints: Bab-el-Mandeb Strait
paths.why_it_matters: Bab-el-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and Arabian Sea, forming the southern gateway to the Suez Canal/SUMED corridor for traffic between the Persian Gulf, Europe, and North America. The strait is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point, with shipping confined to two roughly 2-mile-wide channels, so any closure forces tankers on a much longer detour around the southern tip of Africa, adding transit time and cost.
historical_precedents: Beginning in November 2023, attacks on commercial vessels transiting the Red Sea prompted widespread rerouting; EIA data show oil flows through Bab-el-Mandeb fell from an average of 8.7 million barrels per day in 2023 to about 4.0 million barrels per day in the first eight months of 2024, a roughly 54% decline, while Cape of Good Hope traffic rose from 6.0 to 9.2 million barrels per day over the same comparison.
paths.estimated_global_share: Bab-el-Mandeb carried about 4.2 million barrels per day of oil in 1H2025, down sharply from 6.2 million barrels per day in 2018 (about 9% of seaborne-traded petroleum in 2017), reflecting the post-2023 decline in Red Sea transits, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

paths.name: U.S. Gulf Coast LNG Exports to Europe and Asia
chokepoints: Panama Canal
Strait of Gibraltar
Suez Canal
paths.why_it_matters: The United States became the world's largest LNG exporter, with the great majority of that capacity concentrated in Gulf Coast terminals in Texas and Louisiana. European buyers took over half of U.S. LNG exports in 2024, making this route a central pillar of European gas security since 2022, while Asian buyers (Japan, South Korea, India, China) took roughly a third, so any Gulf Coast terminal outage or Panama Canal transit constraint can tighten global LNG supply and prices simultaneously in two large demand markets.
historical_precedents: A fire at the Freeport LNG terminal on June 8, 2022 forced a full shutdown that removed about 2 billion cubic feet per day, or roughly 17% of total U.S. LNG export capacity, from the market, with the facility only partially restarting months later.

Drought-driven transit restrictions at the Panama Canal in 2023-2024 (daily crossings cut from a typical 34-36 to as low as 24) slowed U.S. Gulf Coast-to-Asia LNG carrier traffic and pushed Gulf Coast-to-Asia gas carrier freight rates to record levels.
paths.estimated_global_share: The U.S. exported a record average of 11.9 billion cubic feet per day of LNG in 2024, remaining the world's largest LNG exporter; Europe took 53% (6.3 Bcf/d) and Asia took 33% (4.0 Bcf/d) of those exports, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

paths.name: Panama Canal Oil and LNG Transit Route
chokepoints: Panama Canal
paths.why_it_matters: The Panama Canal is the primary shortcut connecting U.S. Gulf Coast energy exporters, particularly LNG and LPG carriers, to Asian markets without a much longer voyage around South America. Because the canal is a freshwater lock system dependent on rainfall-fed reservoir levels, it is exposed to drought conditions in ways that ocean straits are not, giving it a distinct and recurring vulnerability among global chokepoints.
historical_precedents: A severe drought dropped Gatun Lake to its lowest level since at least 1965, prompting the Panama Canal Authority to cut daily transit slots from a typical 34-36 to 24 by November 2023; very large gas carrier freight rates on the Houston-Chiba route hit a record $250 per ton in the week ending September 29, 2023, before the Authority restored slots to 35 per day by August 2024 as rains returned.
paths.estimated_global_share: About 2.3 million barrels per day of oil and refined products transited the Panama Canal in FY2025 (roughly 3% of total global maritime petroleum flows), most of it refined products rather than crude, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

paths.name: Central Asia-China Natural Gas Pipeline System
chokepoints: Central Asia-China gas pipeline (Lines A/B/C)
destination_regions: China (Xinjiang and onward via national grid)
paths.why_it_matters: This overland pipeline system is one of the world's longest gas pipeline networks and is China's principal piped-gas supply route, moving gas roughly 1,833 kilometers across Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Kazakhstan into Xinjiang. Unlike maritime chokepoints, its risk profile centers on upstream field capacity, transit-country relations, and infrastructure reliability rather than shipping-lane security, giving it a materially different disruption pattern from the tanker routes above.
historical_precedents: The pipeline's first line opened in December 2009, roughly two years after construction began in August 2007; a second line was completed by the end of 2010, illustrating how new capacity was added in stages over more than a decade.
paths.estimated_global_share: China imported about 35 billion cubic meters of natural gas via three pipeline lines from Turkmenistan in 2022, and the pipeline system's combined nominal capacity is about 55 billion cubic meters per year (with a fourth line planned to raise this to 85 bcm/year), per the Turkmenistan Ministry of Foreign Affairs and industry infrastructure trackers.

paths.name: DRC Cobalt to Global Battery Supply Chains
origin_regions: Democratic Republic of the Congo (Katanga/Lualaba copper-cobalt belt)
chokepoints: Single-country mine-supply concentration in the DRC
Single-country refining dominance in China, which processes most partially refined DRC cobalt into battery-grade chemicals
DRC government export licensing/quota system (in force since October 2025)
destination_regions: East Asia, Europe, and North America (battery and superalloy manufacturing)
paths.why_it_matters: The DRC supplies the large majority of the world's mined cobalt, and China refines most of it into the battery-grade chemicals used in lithium-ion EV and electronics batteries, as well as into materials for aerospace superalloys. Because both the mining and refining stages are each concentrated in a single country, a disruption at either point can quickly affect battery cell costs and superalloy supply for jet engines. A 2025 DRC export ban followed by an export quota system demonstrated how quickly a single government policy can tighten global cobalt supply.
historical_precedents: In August 2019, Glencore announced it would suspend production at the Mutanda mine in the DRC — then the source of roughly one-fifth of global cobalt supply — citing low prices and rising costs; cobalt prices rose more than 30% in the weeks following the announcement.

From February 2025 to October 2025, the DRC suspended all cobalt exports in response to a price collapse (cobalt hydroxide prices had fallen to nine-year lows); the ban was replaced in October 2025 by an annual export quota system (96,600 tonnes for 2026-2027, roughly half of 2024 mine production levels) explicitly intended to tighten supply and stabilize prices.
paths.estimated_global_share: the DRC accounted for an estimated 76% of world cobalt mine production in 2024 (220,000 of 290,000 metric tons), per the U.S. Geological Survey

paths.name: Chile and Peru Copper Exports to Global Markets
chokepoints: Single-country smelting concentration in China, which smelts roughly half of the world's mined copper
Recurring community and labor blockades at major Andean mines
Pacific sea lanes carrying concentrate and cathode exports to Asian smelters
destination_regions: East Asia, Europe, and North America (electronics, construction, grid, and EV manufacturing)
paths.why_it_matters: Chile and Peru together supply roughly a third of the world's mined copper, and copper is a foundational input for electrical grids, construction wiring, and electric vehicles. China has become the dominant smelter of this ore, meaning both the mine-supply and midstream-processing stages are geographically concentrated; the IEA has warned that growing smelting concentration could leave miners more dependent on a single processing hub.
historical_precedents: In April 2022, community blockades forced Peru's Las Bambas mine — a supplier of roughly 2% of world copper — to suspend operations, part of a wider wave of protest-driven disruptions to Peruvian copper output that year.

The COMEX copper price hit a record high in May 2024, which USGS attributed partly to expectations of tighter future global supply, strong Chinese manufacturing activity, and decreasing U.S. inflation.
paths.estimated_global_share: Chile and Peru together accounted for an estimated 34% of world copper mine production in 2024 (Chile about 23%, Peru about 11%, of 23,000 thousand metric tons world total), per the U.S. Geological Survey

paths.name: Australia Iron Ore Exports to China/East Asia Steelmaking
chokepoints: Pilbara rail-and-port export corridor (Port Hedland/Dampier)
Buyer concentration in China's steelmaking industry
Cyclone-season disruptions to Western Australian ports and rail lines
paths.why_it_matters: Australia is the largest source of the seaborne iron ore that feeds China's and East Asia's blast-furnace steel industry. Steel underpins construction, shipbuilding, and automotive manufacturing worldwide, so a disruption to Pilbara mining or export logistics, or a shift in Chinese steel demand, has an outsized effect on global steel and iron-ore prices.
historical_precedents: On 25 January 2019, the failure of a tailings dam at Vale's Corrego do Feijao mine in Brazil (the Brumadinho disaster) forced Vale to curtail iron-ore output; global iron-ore spot prices jumped in the following days on supply concerns, increasing reliance on Australian exporters as the leading alternative supplier.

In November 2025, the Simandou project in Guinea — one of the world's largest untapped high-grade iron-ore deposits — shipped its first export cargo, an early step toward diversifying global iron-ore supply that has historically been concentrated in Australia and Brazil.
paths.estimated_global_share: Australia accounted for an estimated 37% of world iron ore mine production in 2024 (930,000 of 2,500,000 thousand metric tons of usable ore), per the U.S. Geological Survey

paths.name: Indonesia Nickel Exports for Stainless Steel and EV Batteries
chokepoints: Indonesia's ore-export ban (in force since January 2020), which requires ore to be smelted domestically before export
Concentration of new nickel-smelting capacity built with Chinese investment
destination_regions: China (nickel pig iron and stainless steel)
global stainless steel and EV battery (NMC cathode) manufacturing
paths.why_it_matters: Indonesia now supplies the majority of the world's mined nickel, used both in stainless steel and in nickel-based EV battery cathodes. Its 2020 ban on unprocessed ore exports forced processing onshore, concentrating midstream smelting capacity in Indonesia (largely Chinese-financed); the resulting supply surge has repeatedly driven global nickel prices down and pushed higher-cost producers elsewhere out of the market.
historical_precedents: Indonesia banned exports of unprocessed nickel ore starting January 2020 to force domestic smelter development; the policy drove a large buildout of processing capacity, much of it Chinese-financed.

Per USGS, global nickel mine production in 2024 was estimated to have decreased even as Indonesian output rose about 8%, while production fell an estimated 26% in Australia and 20% in the Philippines after companies halted output amid declining prices linked to Indonesian supply growth.
paths.estimated_global_share: Indonesia accounted for an estimated 59% of world nickel mine production in 2024 (2,200,000 of 3,700,000 metric tons), per the U.S. Geological Survey

paths.name: China's Dominance in Rare Earth Element Processing and Export
commodities: rare earths (neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, terbium, and related elements)
origin_regions: Myanmar, Australia, and the United States (mining)
chokepoints: Single-country dominance of separation/refining, about 91% of global output
Single-country dominance of permanent-magnet manufacturing, about 94% of global output
Chinese export-licensing controls on rare-earth materials and related processing technology
destination_regions: global EV motor, wind turbine, electronics, and defense-system manufacturing
paths.why_it_matters: Rare earth elements, especially neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium, are essential inputs for the permanent magnets used in EV motors, wind turbines, and precision electronics. China's dominance extends well beyond mining into the separation, refining, and magnet-manufacturing stages, making this one of the most concentrated of all critical mineral supply chains and giving a single country outsized influence over global magnet supply and pricing.
historical_precedents: In September 2010, China curtailed rare-earth exports to Japan amid a diplomatic dispute; the restriction was followed by a sharp spike in global rare-earth prices and prompted Japan, the United States, and the European Union to pursue supply diversification and stockpiling policies.
In April 2025, new Chinese export controls on rare-earth elements caused temporary production halts in the global automotive industry, according to the International Energy Agency.
paths.estimated_global_share: China accounted for about 60% of global mining output of magnet-related rare earths in 2024, about 91% of global separation/refining output, and about 94% of sintered permanent-magnet production, per International Energy Agency analysis; separately, USGS estimates China produced about 69% of all rare-earth-oxide-equivalent mine output in 2024

paths.name: South America's Lithium Triangle (Chile, Argentina, Bolivia)
chokepoints: Brine evaporation processing, which involves multi-month to multi-year extraction cycles that limit rapid supply response
Government resource-policy shifts, such as Chile's 2023 National Lithium Strategy and Bolivia's state lithium monopoly
Downstream battery-chemical processing concentrated in China
destination_regions: global EV and grid-storage battery manufacturing
paths.why_it_matters: The high-altitude salt-flat brines of Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia hold a large share of the world's identified lithium resources, and Chile and Argentina are already major current producers. Lithium is the primary input for the lithium-ion batteries used in EVs and grid storage, a market USGS reports grew global lithium consumption by 29% in 2024, so policy shifts or production shortfalls in this region can affect global battery-grade lithium pricing.
historical_precedents: In April 2023, Chilean President Gabriel Boric announced a National Lithium Strategy giving the state a controlling role in future lithium projects in Chile, the world's second-largest lithium producer, raising investor questions about future access to Chile's reserves.

Argentina's lithium mine production rose sharply in 2024, to an estimated 18,000 metric tons from 8,630 tons in 2023 (an increase of about 109%), reflecting rapid expansion of new brine projects, per USGS.
paths.estimated_global_share: Chile and Argentina together accounted for an estimated 28% of world lithium mine production in 2024 (Chile about 20%, Argentina about 8%, of 240,000 metric tons world total); Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile together hold roughly half of the world's approximately 115 million tons of identified lithium resources, per the U.S. Geological Survey

paths.name: Guinea Bauxite Exports for Global Aluminum Production
chokepoints: Guinea's dominance of global bauxite reserves and mine output
Heavy customer concentration in Chinese alumina refineries, which receive roughly 70% of Guinea's bauxite exports
Political-stability risk concentrated in a single supplier country
destination_regions: global aluminum smelting for transportation, construction, and packaging
paths.why_it_matters: Guinea holds the world's largest bauxite reserves and was the leading source of mined bauxite in 2024, the raw material refined into alumina and then smelted into aluminum. The large majority of Guinea's bauxite exports go to China's alumina refineries, so a disruption to Guinea's mining or export operations can quickly tighten global alumina supply and raise aluminum prices, affecting industries from auto manufacturing to packaging.
historical_precedents: In September 2021, a coup in Guinea raised concerns about potential disruption to bauxite exports; London Metal Exchange aluminum prices rose to their highest level in roughly a decade in the following days, even though Guinean bauxite shipments continued largely uninterrupted.
paths.estimated_global_share: Guinea accounted for an estimated 29% of world bauxite mine production in 2024 (130,000 of 450,000 thousand metric dry tons) and holds about 26% of world bauxite reserves, per the U.S. Geological Survey; roughly 70% of Guinea's bauxite exports go to China, per industry trade reporting

paths.name: Morocco Phosphate Export Corridor (OCP Group)
origin_regions: Khouribga, Gantour, and Ouled Abdoun phosphate basins, Morocco
chokepoints: Jorf Lasfar deepwater port, Morocco
Safi port, Morocco
Strait of Gibraltar and Atlantic Ocean shipping lanes
paths.why_it_matters: Morocco holds roughly two-thirds of the world's known phosphate rock reserves, the mineral input for phosphorus fertilizers that support root growth and crop yields worldwide. Nearly all Moroccan phosphate rock and its downstream phosphoric acid and fertilizer products move through two Atlantic-coast port complexes, Jorf Lasfar and Safi, concentrating global supply into a narrow logistics footprint. Because phosphorus has no agricultural substitute and reserves are geographically concentrated in a handful of countries, disruption to Moroccan mining, processing, or port operations would have an outsized effect on fertilizer availability and cost for farmers in phosphorus-import-dependent regions such as South Asia, Latin America, and Sub-Saharan Africa.
historical_precedents: September-October 2024: Hurricanes Helene and Milton flooded phosphate mines and processing plants in central Florida, closing several facilities for up to two weeks and halting fertilizer shipments; U.S. phosphate rock imports rose an estimated 35% in 2024 as domestic output was curtailed, illustrating how disruption to any major phosphate-producing region reshapes global trade flows (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).

2024-2028: Phosphate rock and phosphoric acid capacity expansions were underway in Morocco alongside Brazil, Kazakhstan, Mexico, and Russia, part of a projected rise in global phosphate (P2O5) production capacity from 65.0 million tons in 2024 to 70.6 million tons by 2028 to meet rising world fertilizer demand (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).
paths.estimated_global_share: Morocco holds an estimated 50 billion metric tons of the world's roughly 74 billion metric tons of phosphate rock reserves - about 68% of the global total - per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025.

paths.name: Canada (Saskatchewan) Potash Export Network
origin_regions: Saskatchewan potash mining region, Canada (nine mines operated by Nutrien and Mosaic)
chokepoints: Rail corridor from Saskatchewan to Port of Vancouver, British Columbia and Portland, Oregon (~2,000 km)
Rail corridor from Saskatchewan to Saint John, New Brunswick (~4,300 km) and Thunder Bay, Ontario
Marine terminals: Neptune Bulk Terminals (Vancouver), Portland Bulk Terminals, Saint John Terminal, Thunder Bay Terminals
St. Lawrence Seaway / Great Lakes shipping route
paths.why_it_matters: Saskatchewan holds the world's largest potash reserves, and essentially all of it reaches world markets through one coordinated logistics chain: unit trains up to 205 railcars long haul ore roughly 2,000 to 4,300 km to a handful of dedicated port terminals, from which export vessels call at more than 130 ports worldwide each year. Canpotex, the joint export marketer owned by Nutrien and Mosaic, moves about 15 million tonnes of potash annually on behalf of shareholders that together account for a large share of Canadian output. Because potassium has no agricultural substitute and this rail-and-port network carries such a concentrated share of global supply, a prolonged rail, port, or labor disruption in Saskatchewan or its export corridors would directly constrain fertilizer availability for farmers on multiple continents.
historical_precedents: 2018: Canpotex completed a $150 million expansion of Portland Bulk Terminals in Oregon, adding a new shiploader and warehouse capacity to increase throughput of Canadian potash exports (Canpotex).

2020-2022: The USGS-tracked average potash price (f.o.b. mine, K2O equivalent) rose from about $850 per metric ton in 2020 to about $1,790 per ton in 2022 before easing to roughly $1,220 per ton by 2024; Canada increased sales in 2024 to meet growth in world consumption and remained the world's leading potash exporter (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).
paths.estimated_global_share: Canada holds an estimated 1.1 billion metric tons of the world's more than 4.8 billion metric tons of potash reserves (K2O equivalent) - about 23% - and produced about 31% of world potash output in 2024 (15.0 million of 48.0 million tonnes), making it the world's leading potash exporter, per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025.

paths.name: Russia and Belarus Potash Export Corridor
chokepoints: Baltic Sea ports (historically the port of Klaipeda, Lithuania; currently Russian Baltic ports)
Rail corridors from Belarus to China
Black Sea and Baltic Sea shipping lanes
paths.why_it_matters: Russia and Belarus together account for roughly a third of world potash production and reserves, making their export logistics material to global fertilizer supply and price levels. Both countries' potash historically moved to world markets substantially through Baltic Sea ports, so changes in port access, sanctions status, or available shipping and rail routes affect the volume and cost of potash reaching farmers, particularly in Asia and Latin America. Because potassium fertilizer has no agricultural substitute, shifts in Russian or Belarusian export volumes and routing have coincided with measurable global potash price swings.
historical_precedents: 2022: The European Union and the United States placed sanctions on Belarus's state-run potash exporter, and Lithuania terminated the rail transit contract that had allowed Belarus to export potash through the port of Klaipeda; Belarusian potash exports fell sharply as a result (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).

2023-2024: Belarus rerouted potash exports through several Russian ports and increasingly by rail, primarily to China; by 2024 Belarusian production had almost returned to pre-2022 levels even though export volumes via traditional routes remained well below earlier levels (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).

2020-2022: The USGS-tracked average potash price (f.o.b. mine, K2O equivalent) rose from about $850 per metric ton in 2020 to about $1,790 per ton in 2022 amid these and other global supply disruptions, before easing to about $1,220 per ton by 2024 (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).
paths.estimated_global_share: Russia and Belarus together produced an estimated 16.0 million of the world's 48.0 million tonnes of potash in 2024 (about 33%) and hold a combined 1.67 billion of the world's more than 4.8 billion ton K2O-equivalent reserve base (about 35%), per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025.

paths.name: Global Nitrogen/Ammonia Fertilizer Trade (Natural-Gas-Linked Production)
origin_regions: Middle East (Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Iran)
chokepoints: Strait of Hormuz
Gulf of Mexico / Mississippi River shipping and barge system
Caribbean shipping lanes from Trinidad and Tobago
paths.why_it_matters: Ammonia, the building block of nitrogen fertilizer, is manufactured from natural gas, so production is concentrated in regions with low-cost gas feedstock: the US Gulf Coast, Trinidad and Tobago, Russia, and the Middle East. Its trade is exposed both to natural gas price volatility and to shipping-route risk, since an estimated 23% of world ammonia trade and 34% of world urea trade transits the Strait of Hormuz, a single maritime chokepoint linking Gulf-state producers to global markets. Nitrogen fertilizer has no agricultural substitute, so gas-price spikes or shipping disruption along these routes translate quickly into higher costs for farmers, particularly for nitrogen-intensive crops such as corn.
historical_precedents: 2020-2022: US Gulf Coast ammonia prices, as tracked by USGS/Green Markets, rose from an average of $213 per short ton in 2020 to $1,070 per short ton in 2022 amid natural gas price increases and broader fertilizer supply disruption, before easing to about $440 per ton by 2024 (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).

2020-2023: Trinidad and Tobago supplied 51% of US ammonia imports and Canada supplied 47%, together accounting for effectively all US ammonia import volume over that period (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).
paths.estimated_global_share: The Strait of Hormuz corridor carries an estimated 23% of global ammonia trade, 34% of global urea trade, 49% of global sulfur trade, and 18% of global MAP/DAP trade, per the International Fertilizer Association's IFASTAT statistics platform (accessed 2026).

origin_regions: Black Sea region grain-growing areas (Pontic steppe farmland bordering the Black Sea)
chokepoints: Black Sea seaports (including Odesa, Chornomorsk, and Yuzhny/Pivdennyi)
Turkish Straits / Bosphorus
paths.why_it_matters: The Black Sea region is one of the world's most important sources of exportable wheat, corn, and sunflower oil, and many low-income, food-import-dependent countries rely on it to meet basic consumption needs. Because exportable grain supply is concentrated in a small number of origin countries globally, a disruption to Black Sea shipping lanes can quickly tighten world wheat and corn supplies and push up prices for import-dependent economies, with knock-on effects for food-security and inflation in the most vulnerable countries.
historical_precedents: A 2010 drought across Black Sea grain-growing areas, combined with a subsequent export restriction imposed by a leading regional exporter, caused international wheat prices to rise 60-80 percent between the beginning of July and September 2010, according to the FAO's Crop Prospects and Food Situation report (No. 3, September 2010).

A 2022-2023 disruption to shipping lanes in the Black Sea region led the World Bank's April 2022 Commodity Markets Outlook to forecast wheat prices rising more than 40 percent to a nominal all-time high that year, while an FAO information note projected that the resulting global grain and sunflower-seed supply gap could push international food and feed prices 8 to 22 percent above already-elevated levels.

A multilateral agreement brokered in Istanbul in July 2022 enabled the export of more than 32 million metric tons of grain and food products from three Black Sea ports over about a year (including over 725,000 metric tons of wheat shipped under the UN World Food Programme), before the arrangement lapsed in July 2023; by the end of 2022, global wheat prices had returned to pre-disruption levels as shipping patterns and supplier sourcing adapted, per World Bank analysis.
paths.estimated_global_share: FAO's 2022 information note found that, in 2021, Black Sea region exporters ranked among the top three global suppliers of wheat, maize, rapeseed, sunflower seeds, and sunflower oil; separately, World Bank analysis found one of the region's economies alone accounted for roughly 6 percent of global wheat exports by volume (about 10 percent including corn and sunflower seeds) prior to the 2022 disruption.

paths.name: US Midwest Grain Exports via Mississippi River / Gulf of Mexico
origin_regions: US Midwest / Corn Belt farm states (e.g. Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Nebraska, Minnesota)
chokepoints: Mississippi River lock-and-dam and barge system
Port of New Orleans and other Lower Mississippi Gulf export terminals
destination_regions: East and Southeast Asia (including China and Japan)
paths.why_it_matters: Close to 60 percent of US wheat, soybean, and corn exports move by barge down the Mississippi River system to Gulf of Mexico export terminals, making this river-to-port pathway the backbone of US agricultural export competitiveness. Low water levels, lock outages, or other disruptions along the river raise barge freight costs and can delay shipments, affecting both US farm income and buyers worldwide who depend on US grain and oilseed supplies.
historical_precedents: A severe 2012 US drought lowered Mississippi River water levels so much that a towboat and its barges ran aground and forced a channel closure near Greenville, Mississippi in August 2012, backing up close to 100 vessels; the river stage there measured 7.62 feet on August 22, 2012, versus a historic normal of 19.40 feet, and idling towboats incurred costs of nearly $10,000 per day, per NASA Earth Observatory.
paths.estimated_global_share: Close to 60 percent of US grain exports (wheat, soybeans, and corn) travel via the Mississippi River System by barge to the Gulf for export, according to USDA's Agricultural Marketing Service, as reported by Farm Policy News.

paths.name: Brazil Soybean Export Corridor
origin_regions: Mato Grosso, Paraná, Rio Grande do Sul and other Brazilian soybean-growing states
chokepoints: Port of Santos
Port of Paranaguá
Arco Norte (Northern Arc) river/port terminals
paths.why_it_matters: Brazil is the world's largest soybean exporter, and its soybeans feed livestock and edible-oil industries around the world, most importantly in China, which consumes over 60 percent of globally traded soybeans. Weather, logistics, or trade-policy disruptions to Brazil's export pipeline directly affect global animal feed costs and, through them, meat and dairy prices worldwide.
historical_precedents: Tariffs imposed on US soybeans amid 2018 US-China trade tensions accelerated a shift in Chinese purchasing toward Brazil: Brazilian soybean exports to China reached 82 percent of Brazil's total soybean exports in 2018, including a then-record shipment of 2,521 million bushels, while the US share of China's soybean imports fell to just 18 percent that year, according to farmdocdaily analysis of USDA trade data.
paths.estimated_global_share: USDA long-term agricultural projections indicate that Brazil's share of global soybean trade could increase from 51.3 percent in marketing year 2021/22 to 60.6 percent by marketing year 2032/33, with Brazil and the United States together supplying most of the world's soybean exports, per USDA's Economic Research Service.

paths.name: Argentina Soybean Complex Exports (Paraná River / Rosario Hub)
chokepoints: Paraná River shipping channel
Rosario grain port hub
Río de la Plata estuary
destination_regions: global livestock feed and vegetable oil markets
paths.why_it_matters: Argentina is the world's leading exporter of soybean meal and soybean oil, key inputs for global livestock feed and cooking-oil supply chains, even though it ranks behind Brazil and the US in raw soybean exports. Nearly all of this trade is funneled through the Rosario port hub on the Paraná River, so drought, low river levels, or export-policy shifts there have outsized effects on global feed and vegetable-oil prices.
historical_precedents: A 2022/23 drought cut Argentina's soybean harvest by 51.5 percent year-over-year, from 43.3 million tons to 21 million tons — the worst soybean harvest in more than two decades — with yields falling 45 percent to the lowest level in a decade, according to the Buenos Aires Grain Exchange; Argentina's government estimated the drought caused approximately $20 billion in economic losses, nearly 3 percent of GDP.
paths.estimated_global_share: Argentina was forecast to retake its position as the world's largest exporter of soybean meal, with soymeal exports of 27 million metric tons and soy oil exports growing to 5.3 million metric tons in marketing year 2024/25, per a USDA Foreign Agricultural Service GAIN report.

paths.name: Asian Rice Export Corridor (India / Vietnam / Thailand)
chokepoints: Ho Chi Minh City and Bangkok export ports
Strait of Malacca shipping lanes
paths.why_it_matters: Rice is a staple food for more than half the world's population, yet only around 11 percent of global rice production is traded internationally, compared with 16 percent for maize and 27 percent for wheat, so global supply is thin relative to consumption and unusually sensitive to export restrictions by top suppliers. Because exportable rice supply is concentrated in a handful of Asian countries, an export ban or shortfall from any one of them has outsized effects on prices for import-dependent, often lower-income, populations.
historical_precedents: During the 2007-08 rice crisis, export bans, restrictions, and taxes imposed by several major suppliers — including partial bans by Vietnam and India in fall 2007, an export tax announced by China in December 2007, renewed bans by India and Vietnam in March 2008, and minimum export prices set by Pakistan in late April 2008 — helped drive Thailand's benchmark rice export price above $1,000 per ton in late April 2008, more than double its early-February 2008 level and roughly triple year-earlier prices, according to USDA's Economic Research Service.

On July 20, 2023, India banned exports of non-basmati white rice, affecting an estimated 75-80 percent of Indian rice exports, after global rice prices had already risen 15-20 percent since September 2022; India accounted for roughly 40 percent of global rice exports in 2022/23, per an IFPRI analysis.
paths.estimated_global_share: Eight countries — India, Thailand, Vietnam, Pakistan, the United States, China, Burma, and Cambodia — account for about 90 percent of the total volume of annual global rice exports, with India alone (the largest exporter since 2014/15) accounting for around 40 percent of global rice exports in 2022/23, per USDA's Economic Research Service and IFPRI.

paths.name: Global Coffee Export Corridor (Brazil / Vietnam / Colombia)
origin_regions: Minas Gerais and São Paulo states, Brazil (Arabica)
chokepoints: Port of Santos, Brazil
Ho Chi Minh City port, Vietnam
trans-Pacific and trans-Atlantic container shipping lanes
paths.why_it_matters: Coffee export revenue is a major source of foreign exchange and smallholder livelihoods in producing countries, and global supply is concentrated enough that a weather shock in Brazil's growing regions can move world prices within weeks. Because Brazil supplies roughly a third of the world's exported coffee, frost or drought damage to its Arabica crop is transmitted quickly into retail coffee prices worldwide.
historical_precedents: In August 2021, coffee prices recorded a tenth consecutive month of increases, with the ICO composite indicator rising 5.2 percent to 160.14 US cents/lb — a 51.3 percent increase since the start of the 2020/21 coffee year — driven in part by concerns over the size of Brazil's next crop after a severe frost, according to the International Coffee Organization's August 2021 Coffee Market Report.
paths.estimated_global_share: Global coffee exports reached 150 million 60-kg bags in the 2023/24 coffee year; Brazil exported 49.03 million bags (roughly a third of the global total), Colombia exported 11.91 million bags (roughly 8 percent), and the Asia & Oceania region, led by Vietnam, exported 40.62 million bags (27 percent), according to International Coffee Organization data reported via Tridge.

paths.name: Global Sugar Export Corridor (Brazil-centered)
origin_regions: Center-South Brazil sugarcane belt (São Paulo and neighboring states)
chokepoints: Port of Santos, Brazil
Port of Paranaguá, Brazil
paths.why_it_matters: Brazil is the world's largest producer and exporter of sugar, and because Brazilian mills can flexibly divert sugarcane toward either sugar or ethanol production, shifts in Brazilian weather, crushing decisions, or energy policy directly move global sugar supply and prices. Export-restriction decisions by other very large producers, such as India, can compound these swings given how much of world sugar production those countries account for.
historical_precedents: On October 18, 2023, India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry extended restrictions on sugar exports beyond October 31, 2023 to an indefinite period, a policy shift affecting global sugar market expectations given India's position as one of the world's largest sugar producers, according to a USDA Foreign Agricultural Service GAIN report.
paths.estimated_global_share: Brazil is forecast to remain the world's largest producer of sugarcane and sugar in marketing year 2025/26, with total sugarcane production of 671 million metric tons, total sugar production of 44.7 million metric tons (raw value), and sugar exports forecast at 35.8 million metric tons (raw value), according to a USDA Foreign Agricultural Service GAIN report (Sugar Annual, Brazil, April 22, 2025).

paths.name: Taiwan Advanced Semiconductor Foundry to Global Electronics Route
chokepoints: Taiwan Strait shipping and air-freight lanes
Kaohsiung and Taoyuan ports/airport
destination_regions: China and broader East Asia electronics assembly hubs
paths.why_it_matters: A small number of Taiwanese foundries, led by TSMC, fabricate the large majority of the world's most advanced logic chips used in smartphones, PCs, data-center accelerators, and increasingly AI hardware. Because leading-edge chip fabrication requires enormous, hard-to-replicate capital investment and process know-how, any disruption to Taiwan's fabs or their shipping/air-freight routes would ripple through virtually every downstream electronics and automotive industry that depends on current-generation chips.
historical_precedents: COVID-19-era global semiconductor shortage (2020-2022) forced automakers worldwide to idle assembly lines; AlixPartners estimated roughly 7.7 million vehicles' worth of production was lost in 2021 alone, with about $210 billion in lost industry revenue.

March 2021 fire at Renesas Electronics' Naka, Japan chip plant (a major supplier of automotive microcontrollers, though not in Taiwan) illustrated how concentrated a single fab disruption can cascade through global auto supply chains, with Renesas holding roughly 30% of the global microcontroller-chip market at the time.
paths.estimated_global_share: Taiwan accounts for roughly 92% of the world's most advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity, per a 2021 Semiconductor Industry Association/Boston Consulting Group study; CSIS analysis separately describes Taiwan as fabricating on the order of a third of the world's overall computing chip capacity annually.

paths.name: South Korea Memory-Chip (DRAM/NAND) Manufacturing Route
chokepoints: Busan port
East China Sea and Taiwan Strait shipping lanes
destination_regions: China and East Asia electronics assembly hubs
paths.why_it_matters: South Korea's Samsung and SK hynix together dominate global production of DRAM and NAND flash memory, and SK hynix leads in the high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. Memory chips are a commodity input to nearly every computing device and data-center server, so a supply interruption from South Korean fabs has historically caused rapid price spikes across the electronics industry.
historical_precedents: 2021 winter storm-related power outages in Texas, USA disrupted Samsung's Austin fab (outside South Korea) for weeks, illustrating how even geographically diversified memory production is vulnerable to single-site outages given the concentration of advanced memory fabrication in a handful of companies.

2011 Thailand floods disrupted hard-disk-drive component supply chains and, combined with tight memory markets, contributed to a period of DRAM and storage price volatility that affected PC makers worldwide.
paths.estimated_global_share: Samsung Electronics and SK hynix held a combined roughly 67% share of the global DRAM market by revenue in Q1 2026 (Samsung ~38.6%, SK hynix ~28.8%, per Omdia data), and the two together hold over 50% of the global NAND flash market; SK hynix separately holds a majority (around 58%) of the high-bandwidth memory market.

paths.name: China Electronics and Consumer-Goods Manufacturing Export Route
chokepoints: Strait of Malacca
South China Sea shipping lanes
Yantian, Shanghai, and Ningbo-Zhoushan container ports
destination_regions: Southeast Asia and global retail markets
paths.why_it_matters: China is the world's largest single manufacturing economy and the dominant assembly and component base for consumer electronics, making it the anchor node for global electronics retail supply. Because so much final assembly and component sourcing is concentrated in the Pearl River Delta and Yangtze River Delta clusters, port congestion, factory shutdowns, or shipping disruptions there quickly affect global availability and pricing of electronics and general consumer goods.
historical_precedents: COVID-19 lockdowns in Shanghai and other Chinese manufacturing hubs during 2022 caused extended factory closures and port backlogs that contributed to prolonged global shipping delays and component shortages.

2011 Thailand floods disrupted hard-disk-drive supply chains feeding into China-based electronics assembly, showing how upstream component shocks in the region propagate through Chinese final-assembly manufacturing.
paths.estimated_global_share: China's manufacturing value-added reached about $4.66 trillion in 2023, roughly 28% of the world's total manufacturing output and more than the next three largest manufacturing economies combined, per CSIS ChinaPower analysis of World Bank/national data; China also concentrated about 31% of total world exports of electrical machinery and electronics in 2024, per Observatory of Economic Complexity trade data.

paths.name: Global Automobile and Auto-Parts Just-in-Time Supply Route
chokepoints: Ro-Ro shipping lanes and major auto-export ports (Bremerhaven, Yokohama, Ulsan, Veracruz)
Suez Canal for Asia-Europe and intra-Asia vehicle/parts shipments
paths.why_it_matters: The automotive industry runs on tightly synchronized, just-in-time parts flows across Germany, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, and China, meaning a single missing component class (such as microcontroller chips or wiring harnesses) can halt entire assembly lines with little buffer inventory. Because vehicles combine thousands of parts sourced from multiple countries, disruption to any major exporting country's production or shipping routes has historically caused rapid, large-scale production losses.
historical_precedents: The March 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami in Japan disrupted supplier networks for automotive microcontrollers and other components (including Renesas Electronics output feeding Toyota through tier-one suppliers such as Denso), halting production at multiple automakers worldwide.
The 2020-2022 global semiconductor shortage caused an estimated 7.7 million vehicles' worth of lost production in 2021 alone, per AlixPartners, as automakers could not source automotive-grade chips.
paths.estimated_global_share: Germany, Japan, and South Korea posted the world's largest automotive trade surpluses in 2024 (Japan $104B, Germany $99.1B, South Korea $58.4B), with Germany the single largest car exporter by value at $169B in 2024, per Observatory of Economic Complexity trade data; China led global vehicle production with roughly 31.2 million units in 2024 out of about 92.5 million total, according to OICA-sourced production data.

paths.name: Bangladesh and Vietnam Textile & Apparel Export Route
origin_regions: Ho Chi Minh City and northern industrial zones, Vietnam
chokepoints: Strait of Malacca
Suez Canal (for exports to Europe)
Chittagong and Ho Chi Minh City/Haiphong ports
paths.why_it_matters: Bangladesh and Vietnam are the world's second- and third-largest garment exporters respectively, supplying low-cost apparel to major Western retailers on tight seasonal production schedules. Because these countries' apparel factories are deeply networked into global retail supply chains with thin timing margins, factory-safety incidents, labor disruptions, or shipping delays through the Strait of Malacca or Suez Canal can delay seasonal clothing lines and raise costs across global apparel retail.
historical_precedents: The April 24, 2013 collapse of the Rana Plaza garment-factory building near Dhaka, Bangladesh killed 1,138 workers and injured more than 2,500, prompting the international Accord on Fire and Building Safety and lasting reforms to factory-safety inspection regimes in Bangladesh's garment sector, per the ILO.

The March 2021 six-day grounding of the container ship Ever Given in the Suez Canal delayed numerous Asia-to-Europe apparel and textile shipments alongside other cargo, with estimated global trade disruption of roughly $9-10 billion per day of blockage.
paths.estimated_global_share: Bangladesh held roughly a 7.4% share of world apparel/garment exports in 2023 (about $38 billion), retaining second place globally behind China, while Vietnam held roughly a 6% share (about $31 billion) in third place, per WTO World Trade Statistics data cited in industry trade press; Vietnam's textile and garment exports rose to about $44 billion in 2024, per the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association (VITAS).

paths.name: Suez Canal Asia-Europe Manufactured Goods Route
origin_regions: East Asia (China, South Korea, Taiwan, Japan)
chokepoints: Suez Canal
Bab-el-Mandeb Strait and southern Red Sea approach
paths.why_it_matters: The Suez Canal is the primary direct sea route linking Asian manufacturing hubs to European markets, normally carrying a large share of the containerized manufactured goods (electronics, apparel, auto parts) that move between the two regions. When the canal is blocked or avoided, cargo must reroute around the Cape of Good Hope, adding one to two weeks of transit time and materially raising fuel, insurance, and shipping costs for manufactured-goods trade.
historical_precedents: The container ship Ever Given ran aground and blocked the Suez Canal for six days from March 23-29, 2021, disrupting an estimated $9-10 billion in trade per day of blockage.

Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea beginning in late 2023 caused a sharp diversion of vessels away from the Suez Canal; by 2024 tonnage transiting the canal had fallen by roughly 70%, while vessel arrivals via the Cape of Good Hope surged around 89%, per UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2024.
paths.estimated_global_share: The Suez Canal normally carries roughly 12-15% of global trade and about 25-30% of global container shipping traffic, per the IMF and the Atlantic Council citing maritime trade data; over 80% of world trade by volume moves by sea overall, per UNCTAD.

paths.name: China's Antibiotic and Bulk Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) Manufacturing
commodities: key starting materials and drug intermediates
origin_regions: China (Hebei, Jiangsu, Shandong, Zhejiang, and Hubei chemical- and API-manufacturing clusters)
chokepoints: Single-country concentration of antibiotic API and drug-intermediate production in China
India's own generic-drug export industry depends on Chinese APIs and key starting materials for a large share of its inputs
Limited FDA on-site inspection capacity for the large number of Chinese API facilities
paths.why_it_matters: China controls an estimated 70-80% of global antibiotic API production and roughly 80% of the drug intermediates used worldwide to manufacture APIs, according to the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a bipartisan commission created by the U.S. Congress. Because generic medicines account for the large majority of prescriptions dispensed in the United States and elsewhere, and because API manufacturing for whole drug classes such as penicillin-family antibiotics has become commercially unviable outside China, a disruption at a small number of Chinese facilities can constrain finished-drug supply worldwide with few near-term substitutes.
historical_precedents: From January through May 2008, heparin sodium injectable products contaminated with oversulfated chondroitin sulfate were linked to severe allergic reactions and dozens of reported deaths in the United States; the FDA traced the contaminated active ingredient to a supplier network feeding a Changzhou, China API facility, and Baxter Healthcare recalled affected heparin products, per a U.S. Government Accountability Office review of the FDA's response (GAO-11-95, October 2010).

China's January-April 2020 COVID-19 lockdown measures in Hubei and Shandong provinces, both significant API-manufacturing hubs, disrupted output from Chinese bulk-drug and vitamin factories; because India imports an estimated 65-70% of the APIs it uses to manufacture the generic medicines it exports worldwide, the disruption contributed to API shortages and price increases reported by the Indian pharmaceutical industry in early 2020.

paths.name: India's Generic Drug and Vaccine Manufacturing Export Hub
origin_regions: India (Gujarat, Telangana/Hyderabad, Himachal Pradesh, and Andhra Pradesh pharmaceutical-manufacturing clusters)
chokepoints: India's dependence on China for a large share of the active pharmaceutical ingredients it uses to formulate its own generic exports
Indian government export-licensing controls on APIs and formulations during domestic public-health emergencies
paths.why_it_matters: India is the world's largest supplier of generic medicines by volume, accounting for an estimated 20% of global generic-medicine supply, and fulfills roughly 60% of global vaccine demand, supplying vaccines to more than 150 countries, according to Invest India, the Government of India's national investment-promotion agency. Because India's own formulation industry itself depends heavily on imported Chinese APIs, India functions as a critical midstream link that converts Chinese bulk chemicals into the finished medicines used across much of the developing and developed world, meaning disruptions to either country's supply or to India's own export policy can affect medicine availability on multiple continents simultaneously.
historical_precedents: On 3 March 2020, India's Directorate General of Foreign Trade restricted, with immediate effect, the export of 26 active pharmaceutical ingredients and the formulations made from them - including paracetamol, a group accounting for roughly 10% of India's total pharmaceutical exports - citing concerns about maintaining adequate domestic drug supply amid the emerging COVID-19 pandemic; most of the restrictions were lifted within weeks as supply conditions stabilized.

During India's COVID-19 second wave in 2021, the Serum Institute of India paused most COVID-19 vaccine exports for several months starting in March 2021 to prioritize domestic vaccination needs, delaying scheduled deliveries of tens of millions of AstraZeneca-Oxford (Covishield) doses to the COVAX facility supporting 64 lower-income economies; SII had delivered about 28 million doses to COVAX before the pause and resumed COVAX shipments in November 2021, per Gavi.

paths.name: China's Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) Manufacturing and Export Route
origin_regions: China (Hubei province and broader eastern manufacturing clusters)
chokepoints: China's dominant share of world mask manufacturing and exports
Concentration of non-woven meltblown fabric (the filtration material used in medical masks) production in a small number of countries
Chinese export/customs-clearance procedures introduced in 2020 that temporarily slowed shipments
paths.why_it_matters: China became the world's largest exporter of COVID-19-critical medical products in 2020, shipping about $105 billion of such goods, roughly 2.8 times its 2019 export value, per the World Trade Organization. Because mask, gown, and respirator manufacturing capacity was so heavily concentrated in China entering 2020, the initial domestic surge in Chinese demand during the Hubei outbreak sharply reduced the PPE available to the rest of the world just as global demand was also spiking, producing a near-simultaneous worldwide shortage that the WHO said was endangering health workers.
historical_precedents: On 3 March 2020, the World Health Organization warned that industry and governments needed to increase PPE manufacturing by about 40% to meet global demand, noting that prices for surgical masks had risen sixfold, N95 respirator prices had tripled, and gown prices had doubled since the start of the outbreak, and that WHO alone estimated monthly global needs of about 89 million medical masks, 76 million examination gloves, and 1.6 million goggles for the COVID-19 response.

Trade in goods critical to fighting the pandemic - including face masks, ventilators, and sterilizers - grew 31% globally in 2020, with the top 10 exporting economies supplying about three-quarters of world trade in these products, illustrating how concentrated in a handful of countries, led by China, global PPE production capacity was during the shortage, per WTO trade data.

paths.name: Malaysia's Nitrile and Rubber Medical Glove Manufacturing
chokepoints: Malaysia's dominant share of world nitrile glove production capacity
Concentration of production among a small number of large manufacturers (Top Glove, Hartalega, Kossan, Supermax)
Dependence on migrant labor, which became a labor-standards and trade-compliance chokepoint during 2020-2021
paths.why_it_matters: Malaysia produced approximately 60% of the world's nitrile gloves and supplied about 75% by quantity of non-hard rubber medical gloves imported into the United States in 2020, with no other country holding a comparable share, per the U.S. International Trade Commission. Because medical gloves are a single-use, high-volume consumable with few ready substitutes in clinical settings, a labor, logistics, or production disruption concentrated in one country's glove industry can quickly tighten global hospital and clinic supply, as occurred during the COVID-19 demand surge.
historical_precedents: COVID-19 caused a sharp, sustained surge in global demand for medical gloves starting in 2020, straining Malaysian production capacity and extending buyer lead times and prices industry-wide even as Malaysia's dominant producers ran at high utilization, per the U.S. International Trade Commission's 2021 review of global glove production.

On 15 July 2020, U.S. Customs and Border Protection issued a Withhold Release Order barring imports of disposable gloves made by Top Glove Corporation Bhd and its subsidiary TG Medical, then the world's largest medical glove maker, based on evidence of forced-labor indicators in its Malaysian production; CBP escalated this to a formal forced-labor finding in March 2021 and lifted the restriction in September 2021 after Top Glove paid workers more than $30 million in remediation and improved working conditions.

paths.name: Serum Institute of India Vaccine Manufacturing and Global Immunization Supply
commodities: routine childhood vaccines (DTP, MMR, BCG, hepatitis B, pneumococcal, polio)
origin_regions: India (Pune, Maharashtra - Serum Institute of India manufacturing complex)
chokepoints: Concentration of a large share of global vaccine dose volume in a single company and manufacturing site
Cold-chain logistics required to keep temperature-sensitive vaccines viable from the Pune facility to recipient countries
Dependence of Gavi/COVAX-funded low-income country immunization programs on a single manufacturer
Indian government export-licensing decisions during domestic public-health emergencies
destination_regions: 170 countries via national immunization programs and the COVAX facility
paths.why_it_matters: The Serum Institute of India is the world's largest vaccine manufacturer by number of doses produced and sold, supplying more than one billion vaccine doses per year to children in over 170 countries and providing an estimated 40% of the vaccines funded by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. Because such a large share of the world's routine childhood immunization supply and low-cost pandemic-vaccine capacity is concentrated at a single company's facilities in Pune, any disruption to that site, or any government decision to redirect its output domestically, can directly affect vaccine availability for children in dozens of lower-income countries simultaneously.
historical_precedents: Starting in March 2021, as India's COVID-19 second wave intensified domestic demand, the Serum Institute paused most vaccine exports for several months; on 25 March 2021 Gavi announced that scheduled COVAX deliveries of roughly 40 million Covishield (AstraZeneca-Oxford) doses for March and up to 50 million for April, destined for 64 lower-income economies, would be delayed, after SII had already supplied about 28 million doses to COVAX; SII resumed COVAX shipments in November 2021.

Over Gavi's 2016-2020 strategic period, the Serum Institute supplied more than half a billion vaccine doses for Gavi-supported immunization programs protecting children against nine diseases including measles, rubella, meningitis A, and rotavirus, illustrating the scale of routine (non-pandemic) global immunization programs that rely on this single manufacturer, per Gavi.

paths.name: U.S. Gulf Coast Ethylene and Petrochemical Export Corridor

paths.why_it_matters: The Houston Ship Channel area is the largest concentrated petrochemical manufacturing complex in the world, and cheap U.S. shale-gas-derived ethane has made the Gulf Coast the world's lowest-cost source of ethylene and its plastics derivatives (polyethylene, PVC, ethylene glycol). paths.why_it_matters: China is both the world's largest single producer and largest single consumer of plastics, manufacturing roughly a third of the world's common plastic resins for its own vast packaging, construction, and electronics industries as well as for export. Because so much of this capacity, including a large share of PVC that relies on coal-based calcium carbide rather than oil-based ethylene, is concentrated in a small number of Chinese industrial regions, domestic energy policy or plant outages there can move global resin prices even without any change in Chinese trade policy.
historical_precedents: China's January 2018 'National Sword' policy banned imports of most plastic and other recyclable waste, causing Chinese plastic waste imports to collapse by about 99% and displacing an estimated 111 million metric tons of plastic waste that had previously relied on Chinese processing (95% of EU and 70% of U.S. recyclables had gone to China/Hong Kong before the ban), forcing exporting countries to redirect waste to Southeast Asia or curtail recycling programs domestically, per Yale Environment 360 and Wikipedia's documentation of the policy.

In September 2021, Chinese authorities ordered energy-intensive chemical plants in Ningxia, Xinjiang, and Shaanxi (accounting for a large share of the roughly 80% of China's 25-26 million tons/year PVC capacity that is coal-carbide based) to curtail operations amid a nationwide power crunch, driving Chinese PVC prices to multi-year highs within weeks, per ChemAnalyst.
paths.estimated_global_share: China accounted for approximately 34.5% of total global plastics production in 2024, more than the combined output of the next several largest producing countries, per Statista and Economic Times reporting citing industry (Eunomia) research.

Because this concentration sits far upstream of the chip fabs themselves (in Taiwan, South Korea, and elsewhere), Japanese government export-licensing decisions or a disruption at one of a few specialized plants can constrain semiconductor output worldwide even when fab capacity itself is unaffected.
historical_precedents: In July 2019, Japan's government imposed export controls requiring case-by-case licensing for shipments to South Korea of three chemicals essential to semiconductor and display manufacturing (hydrogen fluoride, photoresist, and fluorinated polyimide); a Research Institute of Economy, Trade and Industry (RIETI) study found the controls caused a large, measurable decline in Japanese hydrogen fluoride exports to South Korea, prompting South Korean firms to shift sourcing toward Belgium, the United States, and Taiwan and to accelerate domestic and China-based production capacity.

paths.name: Indonesia's Thermal Coal Exports to Asia

chokepoints: Indonesia's Domestic Market Obligation (DMO) policy, which can trigger sudden government-ordered export halts

paths.why_it_matters: Indonesia is the world's largest coal exporter by volume, shipping mostly thermal coal to power plants across Asia. Indonesian law requires miners to reserve a minimum share of output for the domestic market at a government-capped price, and a shortfall in that domestic supply can trigger an abrupt, economy-wide halt to exports, as occurred in January 2022. Given Indonesia's outsized share of the seaborne thermal coal market, disruptions of this kind can move global coal prices within days.
historical_precedents: On January 1, 2022, Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources ordered a monthlong halt to coal exports after miners had delivered only about 35,000 of the 5.1 million metric tons owed to domestic power plants under the Domestic Market Obligation, citing the risk that roughly 20 power plants totaling about 10,850 MW of capacity could go offline; the ban was eased in stages from January 20, 2022 as individual companies met their quotas, and international thermal coal prices rose in the interim, per Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources and S&P Global Commodity Insights.
paths.estimated_global_share: Indonesia exported an estimated 555 million tonnes of coal in 2024, the largest volume of any country, as part of a combined 74% global export share held by Indonesia, Australia, and Russia together, per the International Energy Agency's Coal 2025 report.

Japan, China, India, and South Korea together take the large majority of Australian coal exports, so mine, rail, or port disruptions in Australia (frequent during the Queensland cyclone season) or shifts in Asian steel and power demand have an outsized effect on global seaborne coal prices, particularly for metallurgical coal.

paths.name: China's Dominance in Global Solar Panel Manufacturing
origin_regions: China (manufacturing base spanning Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Xinjiang, and other provinces)
chokepoints: Single-country manufacturing concentration exceeding 80% at every stage of production (polysilicon, ingots/wafers, cells, modules)
US and EU trade-remedy tariffs targeting Chinese-linked solar cells and modules
destination_regions: global utility-scale and rooftop solar markets
paths.why_it_matters: China's share of global manufacturing capacity exceeds 80% at every stage of the solar panel supply chain, from polysilicon through finished modules, a level of concentration the IEA has said is unmatched by any other major energy technology or fuel supply chain, including oil, gas, or coal. This gives Chinese industrial and trade policy outsized influence over global solar panel availability and pricing, and has repeatedly prompted the United States and European Union to pursue trade-defense measures and domestic manufacturing incentives aimed at diversifying supply.
historical_precedents: In October 2012, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed final antidumping duties of up to 249.96% and countervailing duties on Chinese-made crystalline silicon solar cells, following an October 2011 petition from SolarWorld and other U.S. manufacturers alleging underpriced Chinese imports were harming the domestic industry; the orders were later expanded to cover Taiwan-assembled cells in 2014.

Effective February 7, 2018, the United States imposed a Section 201 global safeguard tariff of 30% on imported crystalline-silicon solar cells and modules, with an annual duty-free exemption for the first 2.5 gigawatts of imported cells, stepping down five percentage points per year; the measure was extended by four years in 2022.
paths.estimated_global_share: China's share of global manufacturing capacity across polysilicon, ingots/wafers, cells, and modules exceeded 80% as of the IEA's 2022 Special Report on Solar PV Global Supply Chains, with polysilicon and wafer capacity on track to reach almost 95% by 2030 based on capacity under construction; Wood Mackenzie separately estimated China would hold more than 80% of global polysilicon, wafer, cell, and module manufacturing capacity every year from 2023 through 2026.

paths.why_it_matters: After the United States imposed antidumping and countervailing duties on solar cells and modules from China starting in 2012, a large share of cell and module assembly capacity relocated to Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam, which together supplied an estimated 84% of all U.S. solar cell and module imports in the fourth quarter of 2023. paths.why_it_matters: China accounted for roughly 80% of global lithium-ion battery cell production in 2024 and supplies the large majority of the cathode and anode active materials that go into those cells, giving it outsized influence over EV and grid-storage battery costs worldwide. Two Chinese firms, CATL and BYD, alone held a combined majority of the global EV battery market in 2024, and the concentration runs deep enough that even automakers building battery plants in the United States and Europe, such as Ford's Michigan LFP plant, have relied on licensed Chinese cell technology rather than fully independent designs.
historical_precedents: In February 2023, Ford announced a $3.5 billion wholly owned lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery plant in Marshall, Michigan, built using battery technology licensed from China's CATL, illustrating how even U.S.-based, U.S.-owned battery manufacturing has depended on Chinese cell chemistry and process know-how.

Effective December 1, 2023, China's Ministry of Commerce required export permits for high-purity synthetic and spherical natural graphite products used in battery anodes, tightening a chokepoint the IEA says supplies over 90% of global anode active material processing.
paths.estimated_global_share: China accounted for about 80% of global lithium-ion battery cell production in 2024, supplying almost 85% of global cathode active material and over 90% of global anode active material, per the IEA's Global EV Outlook 2025 and Batteries and Secure Energy Transitions report; separately, SNE Research found CATL (37.9%) and BYD (17.2%) together held about 55% of the global EV battery market in 2024.

paths.name: Global Wind Turbine Manufacturing Supply Concentration
chokepoints: Rapid buildout of Chinese domestic wind turbine manufacturing capacity, now roughly 60% of global manufacturing capacity
China's near-total (99.96%) domestic-market self-supply, limiting the pool of turbines independently price-tested outside China
EU Foreign Subsidies Regulation scrutiny of Chinese turbine suppliers bidding into European wind-farm tenders
paths.why_it_matters: Chinese wind turbine manufacturers have risen from about 30% of the global market in 2017 to supplying the five largest annual turbine installers worldwide for the first time in 2025, while the IEA separately estimates China holds roughly 60% of global wind-system manufacturing capacity. Because Chinese OEMs still install over 90% of their own output domestically, most of that capacity has not yet been fully tested in open international competition, and European regulators have opened a formal subsidy investigation into Chinese suppliers winning tenders in EU member states, adding a distinct regulatory chokepoint alongside the underlying manufacturing concentration.
historical_precedents: GWEC data show Chinese wind turbine suppliers' share of global annual installations rising from about 30% in 2017 to 67% of new units installed worldwide in 2025 (18,291 of 28,395 turbines), with Goldwind, Envision, Windey, MingYang, and SANY forming the top five global OEMs by annual capacity installed for the first time.

On April 9, 2024, the European Commission announced the first ex-officio investigation under its Foreign Subsidies Regulation, targeting Chinese wind turbine suppliers bidding into wind-farm tenders in Spain, Greece, France, Romania, and Bulgaria; the Commission escalated to a formal in-depth second-stage investigation into Goldwind's EU activities in February 2026.
paths.estimated_global_share: Chinese manufacturers installed 18,291 of the 28,395 new wind turbines commissioned worldwide in 2025 (67% of units), and supplied the top five original equipment manufacturers by annual capacity installed for the first time, per GWEC; separately, the IEA estimates China holds about 60% of global wind-system manufacturing capacity and roughly half of component exports.
